How the Eukaryotyping distance ensemble works

Angel Luís Robles Fernández

Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology and Center for Ecological Research, University of Kansas
Source: vignettes/algorithm.Rmd
algorithm.Rmd

This vignette explains the three distance methods that make up the Eukaryotyping ensemble. The component methods (heuristic and Bayesian) are faithful reimplementations of the original R scripts from Barratt, Park, Nascimento et al. (2019; doi:10.1017/S0031182019000581), verified to within \(10^{-10}\) on a 68-sample C. cayetanensis HDS fixture. The ensemble "original" mode reproduces the published run.r workflow verbatim; the "rank" mode is a package-specific variant.

Notation

Let:

  • \(n\) be the number of isolates (samples)
  • \(L\) be the number of loci
  • For locus \(j\), \(\mathcal{A}_j\) is the set of observed alleles across all samples
  • For isolate \(i\) and locus \(j\), \(\mathbf{g}_{ij}\) is the multiset of alleles carried by that isolate (size up to \(\text{MOI}_j\), the maximum multiplicity for that locus)
  • \(p_{ja}\) is the empirical frequency of allele \(a\) at locus \(j\)
  • \(H_{\nu j}\) is the entropy of locus \(j\)

1. Heuristic distance (euk_heuristic_distance)

The heuristic distance is Barratt’s unsupervised mixture-model distance. For each pair of isolates \((i, k)\) and each locus \(j\), a per-locus delta \(\delta_{ik}^{(j)}\) is computed; the overall distance is the sum of per-locus deltas. A contribution is missing (no comparable locus) when either isolate has no allele at that locus, not only when both lack it.

Per-locus delta

Let \(S_{ij}\) be the set of distinct alleles carried by isolate \(i\) at locus \(j\). Define:

  • \(x = |S_{ij}| + |S_{kj}|\) — total distinct allele count
  • \(y = |S_{ij} \cap S_{kj}|\) — number of shared distinct alleles
  • \(n = \min(|S_{ij}|, |S_{kj}|)\)
  • \(m_j\) — a per-locus tuning parameter (default 1)

A frequency-informed penalty \(P\) moderates the contribution of shared alleles that are rare:

\[ P = \begin{cases} \Bigl(\frac{\#\{r : S_{ij} \cap S_{kj} \subseteq S_{rj}\}}{n_{\text{nonmissing},j}}\Bigr)^2 & y > 0 \\[4pt] 1 & y = 0 \end{cases} \]

where \(n_{\text{nonmissing},j}\) is the number of isolates with at least one non-missing allele at locus \(j\).

The per-locus delta for diploid loci (\(\text{ploidy} > 1\)) is:

\[ \delta = H_{\nu j} \cdot \Bigl( \delta_{\text{raw}} \cdot \mathbb{I}(\delta_{\text{raw}} > 0) + P \cdot \mathbb{I}(\delta_{\text{raw}} = 0) \Bigr) \cdot k \]

where \(k = 1\) if \(y = 0\) and \(k = P\) otherwise, and \(\delta_{\text{raw}}\) is a piecewise integer function of \(x\), \(y\), \(n\), and \(m_j\) that implements the original Barratt lookup table (see src/eukaryotyping.cpp:sub_per_locus() for the exact mapping).

For haploid loci the expression retains the same structure:

\[ \delta = H_{\nu j} \cdot \bigl( \delta_{\text{ex,raw}} \cdot \mathbb{I}(\delta_{\text{ex,raw}} > 0) + P \cdot \mathbb{I}(\delta_{\text{ex,raw}} = 0) \bigr) \cdot k \]

with \(\delta_{\text{ex,raw}} = 2x\) when \(y = 0\) and \(\delta_{\text{ex,raw}} = 0\) otherwise. When \(y > 0\) the \(P\) replacement term contributes \(H_{\nu j} \cdot P^2\) — shared alleles do not give a zero contribution. The entropy \(H_{\nu j}\) is the Shannon entropy of the empirical allele distribution:

\[ H_{\nu j} = -\sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_j} p_{ja} \log_2 p_{ja} \]

Preprocessing and diagonal

The R reference (euk_heuristic_distance_r) and the C++ implementation preprocess each locus by converting 0 to NA and replicating the single observed allele into both columns for diploid loci with MOI = 1. Donor matching during imputation compares the post-preprocessing empty-slot patterns, so two isolates that agree on their non-missing alleles but differ in whether a singleton diploid was replicated are not considered matches.

Self-pairs (the diagonal) are computed through the full per-locus delta machinery and are not forced to zero — a heterozygous diploid individual has a non-zero within-sample distance.

Missing-locus imputation

Barratt’s two-pass mean procedure fills entries where a locus is missing for an isolate:

  1. For each isolate with a missing locus, find all complete isolates whose post-preprocessing allele sets and fullness flags match at every non-missing locus. Impute the missing-locus delta as the mean of those matched isolates’ deltas.
  2. If no match exists, impute using the global mean of the locus.
  3. A second pass catches any rows that remain partially empty after the first pass, re-imputing against the first-pass results.

The final distance for pair \((i, k)\) is:

\[ D_{ik}^{(H)} = \sum_{j=1}^{L} \delta_{ik}^{(j)} \]

2. Bayesian distance (euk_bayesian_distance)

Plucinski’s naive-Bayes distance evaluates, for each pair \((i, k)\), three log-likelihoods per locus corresponding to three relatedness hypotheses. If a pair has no comparable locus (each locus is unobserved for at least one member) the method skips all loci (via colSums(..., na.rm = TRUE)) and returns exactly \(1.0\) — a uniform posterior — rather than imputing.

The Bayesian functions do not preprocess by duplicating diploid singleton alleles (unlike the heuristic path), so an isolate with a single observed allele at a diploid locus contributes one allele instead of two.

Per-locus log-likelihoods

Let \(\mathbf{v}_{ij}\) be the allele values (not the set, but the actual observed alleles, with multiplicities) carried by isolate \(i\) at locus \(j\), and let \(p_{ja}\) be the empirical frequency of allele \(a\) as above.

Hypothesis 0 — unrelated:

Both isolates draw all their alleles independently from the locus allele frequencies:

\[ \ell_0 = \sum_{a \in \mathbf{v}_{ij}} \log p_{ja} + \sum_{a \in \mathbf{v}_{kj}} \log p_{ja} \]

Hypothesis 1 — share one allele:

The pair shares exactly one allele; the shared allele is the most likely one. For every pair of positions \((u, v)\) where \(v_{iju} = v_{kjv}\), compute:

\[ \ell_{1,uv} = \ell_0 - \log p_{j,v_{iju}} \]

and take \(\ell_1 = \max_{uv} \ell_{1,uv}\). If no shared allele exists, \(\ell_1 = \log(\epsilon \cdot \min(p_{\text{obs}}))\), where \(\epsilon\) is the estimated allele-capture failure rate (default 0.3072, estimated by Joel Barratt in May 2019) and \(\min(p_{\text{obs}})\) is the smallest frequency among the alleles carried by the pair.

Hypothesis 2 — share both alleles:

Both isolates share a pair of alleles (multiset equality). For every pair of 2-subsets \((\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})\) from \(\mathbf{v}_{ij}\) and \(\mathbf{v}_{kj}\) that are equal as multisets:

\[ \ell_{2,\mathbf{a}\mathbf{b}} = \sum_{a \in \mathbf{v}_{ij} \setminus \mathbf{a}} \log p_{ja} + \sum_{a \in \mathbf{v}_{kj}} \log p_{ja} \]

which is equivalent to \(\ell_0\) with the log-frequencies of the removed pair elements subtracted (the original R code uses match() to locate the first-position index of each pair value, then removes those indices via negative indexing). Let

\[ n_{\text{shared}} = \max_{\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}} \bigl|\operatorname{intersect}(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})\bigr| \]

be the maximum distinct-allele overlap over all 2-subset combinations.

If a multiset equality is found, \(\ell_2 = \max \ell_{2,\mathbf{a}\mathbf{b}}\). Otherwise:

\[ \ell_2 = \log\bigl[(\epsilon \cdot \min(p_{\text{obs}}))^{2 - n_{\text{shared}}}\bigr] \]

For ploidy 1 loci, and when either allele vector has length 1, the package sets \(\ell_2 = \ell_1\) (a package-level decision — the original script crashes on these cases).

Posterior and distance

The per-locus log-likelihoods are summed across loci:

\[ s_0 = \sum_{j} \ell_0^{(j)}, \quad s_1 = \sum_{j} \ell_1^{(j)}, \quad s_2 = \sum_{j} \ell_2^{(j)} \]

These are normalised to a posterior over the three hypotheses:

\[ \Pr(h \mid \text{data}) = \frac{e^{s_h}}{e^{s_0} + e^{s_1} + e^{s_2}}, \quad h \in \{0, 1, 2\} \]

The distance is the posterior expected number of shared-allele hypotheses:

\[ D_{ik}^{(B)} = 0 \cdot \Pr(0) + 1 \cdot \Pr(1) + 2 \cdot \Pr(2) \in [0, 2] \]

Values near 0 indicate the pair appears unrelated; values near 2 suggest complete allelic sharing. Self-pair diagonals range approximately \(1.46\)–\(2.0\) (a homozygous diploid with common alleles scores near 2; a singleton diploid with a rare allele scores lower).

3. Ensemble distance (euk_ensemble_distance)

The heuristic and Bayesian distances operate on different scales and have different sensitivities. The ensemble combines them via one of two methods chosen with the method argument.

method = "original" (default)

Reproduces the published run.r workflow verbatim:

  1. Reverse the Bayesian direction: \(D_B' = 2 - D_B\) so that both matrices are divergence-oriented (larger = more dissimilar).
  2. Min-max normalise each matrix over all entries (diagonal, upper and lower triangles together) to \([0, 1]\).
  3. Let \(H\) be the normalised heuristic and \(B\) the reversed- normalised Bayesian matrix. Sort \(B\)’s values and map them onto the rank-order of \(H\): \[ D_{ik}^{(E)} = B_{(\text{rank}(H_{ik}))} \] where ties in \(H\) are broken randomly (ties.method = "random"), making the output non-deterministic unless a seed is provided.
  4. Take the elementwise mean of the distribution-mapped matrix and \(H\), then rescale by the global maximum.

Because ties in the heuristic ranking are resolved at random, two calls with the same data can produce different matrices. The output matrix can also be asymmetric (the random tie-breaking and the full-matrix (non-triangular) sorting do not guarantee symmetry).

method = "rank"

A package-specific variant that avoids random tie-breaking and preserves symmetry:

  1. Reverse the Bayesian direction: \(D_B' = 2 - D_B\), so both matrices are divergence-oriented.
  2. For an \(n \times n\) distance matrix \(D\), let \(U\) be the set of \(\binom{n}{2}\) strictly upper-triangular entries. Assign fractional ranks: \[ r(D)_{ik} = \frac{\text{rank of } D_{ik} \text{ among } U} {\binom{n}{2} + 1} \] with ties resolved by ties.method = "average". The diagonal is set to NA.
  3. The ensemble entry is: \[ D_{ik}^{(E)} = \frac{r(D_H)_{ik} + r(D_B')_{ik}}{2} \]

Interpretation

After reversal both components are divergence-oriented:

  • Values near 0 indicate both methods agree on high similarity (low divergence).
  • Values near 1 indicate agreement on strong divergence.

For the "rank" method the output lies in \((0, 1)\); for "original" the range depends on the global min-max scaling. The "rank" method is a package variant and is not described in the original publication.

References

Barratt JLN, Park S, Nascimento FS, et al. (2019) “Genotyping genetically heterogeneous Cyclospora cayetanensis infections to complement epidemiological case linkage”. Parasitology 146:1275–1283. doi:10.1017/S0031182019000581.

Component distances (heuristic and Bayesian) verified against the original R scripts to within \(10^{-10}\) on a 68-sample fixture. The ensemble "rank" method is a package-level extension.
